entities.summary:
Rudolf II von Scherenberg, who presided as Prince-Bishop of Würzburg from 1466 until his death on May 8, 1495, was a pivotal ecclesiastical and political figure in late medieval Franconia. His unusually long tenure of nearly three decades provided remarkable stability and fostered a period of significant artistic and architectural flourishing within his prince-bishopric, a crucial territorial state within the Holy Roman Empire. His reign coincided with the twilight of the Middle Ages and the dawn of the Renaissance in Central Europe, positioning Würzburg as a regional center of cultural and spiritual influence under his patronage.

During his episcopacy, Rudolf von Scherenberg oversaw considerable construction and renovation projects, notably the strengthening of Marienberg Fortress and the embellishment of Würzburg Cathedral. He was a discerning patron of the arts, most famously commissioning the renowned sculptor Tilman Riemenschneider to create his own monumental tomb effigy, a masterpiece of late Gothic sculpture completed around 1499. Beyond cultural endeavors, Scherenberg navigated complex political landscapes, maintaining relative peace and prosperity for his territories amidst the broader machinations of the Imperial Diet and the shifting power dynamics among German princes, including Emperor Frederick III. He also addressed internal reforms within the diocese, working to improve monastic discipline and clerical education.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Rudolf von Scherenberg's nearly three-decade reign provided significant stability and fostered a vibrant period of artistic patronage in the Prince-Bishopric of Würzburg, most notably through his commissions to Tilman Riemenschneider, leaving an enduring cultural legacy for the region.
